Phần A

1. Governments are trying to find new ways to MITIGATE the harmful effects of rising sea levels on coastal communities. --- MITIGATE (động từ) = giảm thiểu, làm dịu bớt mức độ nghiêm trọng của một tác động tiêu cực; collocation phổ biến: "mitigate the effects of", "mitigate a risk"; đừng nhầm với "militate against" (cản trở).

2. The clearing of large areas of tropical forest is reducing the BIODIVERSITY found there. --- BIODIVERSITY (danh từ không đếm được) = đa dạng sinh học; collocation: "a loss of biodiversity", "biodiversity conservation"; không có dạng số nhiều.

3. Scientists warn that once certain ecosystems collapse, the damage will become completely IRREVERSIBLE. --- IRREVERSIBLE (tính từ) = không thể đảo ngược, không thể khắc phục; tiền tố phủ định là "ir-" (không phải "un-reversible"); collocation: "irreversible damage/consequences".

4. DEFORESTATION in the Amazon is one of the main drivers of global carbon emissions. --- DEFORESTATION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự phá rừng trên diện rộng; collocation: "massive/rampant deforestation", "curb deforestation"; phân biệt với "afforestation" (trồng rừng mới) và "reforestation" (trồng lại rừng).

5. URBAN SPRAWL is destroying natural habitats and farmland around the city. --- URBAN SPRAWL (danh từ không đếm được) = sự đô thị hoá tràn lan, thiếu kiểm soát; collocation: "unchecked urban sprawl", "urban sprawl encroaches on"; đối lập với "urban planning".

6. Flying less and eating locally produced food are two simple ways to reduce your CARBON FOOTPRINT. --- CARBON FOOTPRINT (danh từ ghép, đếm được) = tổng lượng khí thải nhà kính do một cá nhân/tổ chức gây ra; collocation: "reduce/calculate one's carbon footprint"; không viết tách "carbon-footprint" khi làm danh từ.

7. The steady DEPLETION of the region's groundwater supplies is threatening the long-term water security of local farmers. --- DEPLETION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự cạn kiệt dần một nguồn tài nguyên; luôn cần giới từ "of" khi nêu tài nguyên cụ thể ("the depletion of resources"); collocation: "resource depletion", "ozone depletion".

8. Decades of unchecked industrial pollution have caused severe DEGRADATION of the local wetland. --- DEGRADATION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự suy thoái, quá trình môi trường xuống cấp; collocation: "environmental/land degradation"; phân biệt với "biodegradable" (dễ phân huỷ sinh học, mang nghĩa tích cực).

9. Most climate scientists agree that the recent rise in global temperatures is largely ANTHROPOGENIC rather than the result of natural cycles. --- ANTHROPOGENIC (tính từ) = do con người gây ra; thuật ngữ học thuật trang trọng, có thể thay bằng "man-made"/"human-induced" trong văn nói; collocation: "anthropogenic warming/emissions".

10. The oil company's environmental record has recently COME UNDER SCRUTINY after the spill was made public. --- COME UNDER SCRUTINY (cụm động từ) = bị soi xét, giám sát chặt chẽ; collocation: "come under intense/public scrutiny"; "scrutiny" là danh từ không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều.

11. Researchers warn that the Arctic could soon reach a critical TIPPING POINT beyond which the ice loss becomes self-perpetuating and impossible to reverse. --- TIPPING POINT (danh từ ghép, đếm được) = điểm tới hạn gây ra thay đổi lớn, khó đảo ngược; luôn viết hai từ tách rời; collocation: "reach/cross a tipping point".

12. Several major economies have announced plans to PHASE OUT coal-fired power stations within the next two decades. --- PHASE OUT (cụm động từ) = loại bỏ dần theo lộ trình, không đột ngột; khi làm danh từ viết có gạch nối "a phase-out"; collocation: "phase out fossil fuels".
Phần B

1. Band 6: Factories put a lot of bad gases into the air and this makes global warming worse. - Band 7: Factories release substantial greenhouse gas emissions, which exacerbate global warming. - Band 8: It is the unchecked anthropogenic emissions pouring from industrial facilities that continue to drive global warming to increasingly alarming levels.

2. Band 6: If people keep cutting down trees, many animals will lose their homes. - Band 7: If deforestation continues at its current rate, countless species will lose their natural habitats. - Band 8: Were deforestation to persist unabated, the resulting loss of biodiversity would leave countless species with nowhere left to call home.

3. Band 6: The government should use more solar and wind power instead of coal. - Band 7: The government should invest more heavily in renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, rather than relying on coal. - Band 8: Not until the government commits to phasing out coal in favour of renewable energy will the country make any meaningful progress towards decarbonisation.

4. Band 6: Rich countries caused most of the pollution in the past, so they should help poorer countries now. - Band 7: Since developed nations are historically responsible for the majority of emissions, they ought to support developing countries in tackling climate change. - Band 8: Given that developed economies bear disproportionate historical responsibility for cumulative emissions, it is only equitable that they should shoulder the greater share of the burden in assisting developing nations to mitigate climate change.

5. Band 6: Plastic waste in the ocean is a very big problem and it is getting worse every year. - Band 7: Marine plastic pollution is a serious and worsening problem, with the scale of the crisis increasing year on year. - Band 8: What is most alarming is not merely the scale of marine plastic pollution but the rate at which it continues to escalate, with each passing year bringing the world closer to an ecological tipping point.

6. Band 6: One person recycling more will not really change the whole climate problem. - Band 7: An individual recycling more is, admittedly, just a drop in the ocean compared to the scale of the climate crisis. - Band 8: While one individual's efforts to recycle amount to little more than a drop in the ocean, it is only when such actions are replicated on a mass scale that they can meaningfully mitigate the climate crisis.

7. Band 6: Cities are growing too fast and this is destroying the countryside around them. - Band 7: Cities are expanding at an unsustainable rate, and this unchecked urban sprawl is encroaching on the surrounding countryside. - Band 8: So rapid has urban sprawl become that once-fertile arable land on the city's fringes is being irreversibly swallowed up by concrete and asphalt.

8. Band 6: If nothing changes soon, some of the damage to nature will never be fixed. - Band 7: Unless urgent action is taken, some of the damage inflicted on the natural environment will become irreversible. - Band 8: Failing swift and decisive intervention, we risk crossing tipping points beyond which the degradation of our ecosystems can never be undone.

passages.text: For most of the twentieth century, the dominant framing of climate adaptation on tropical reefs rested on a deceptively simple proposition: reduce local stressors, and the corals will largely look after themselves. That assumption, which informed early marine park legislation in Australia, Belize and the Maldives, is no longer treated as adequate. A new generation of reef ecologists has begun to argue that the response of corals to repeated marine heatwaves is mediated not only by water quality and fishing pressure but by the communities of bacteria, viruses and microalgae living within the coral tissue itself. The implications of this microbial turn, several commentators contend, extend well beyond reef biology into the contested terrain of adaptation policy.

The conceptual basis of the new approach lies in the holobiont model, which treats a coral colony as a single integrated ecosystem comprising the animal polyp, its photosynthetic algal partner and a diverse microbial assemblage. Professor Naledi Khumalo, a marine microbiologist at the University of Cape Town, has characterised the holobiont as "an evolutionary unit that the older taxonomic framework was never designed to capture". Her laboratory has demonstrated that the composition of the bacterial fraction can shift within hours of a thermal stress event, and that some shifts appear to confer measurable tolerance to subsequent heatwaves. Khumalo concedes, however, that the causal pathways remain incompletely resolved, and she has cautioned against premature claims that microbial profiles can be reliably engineered.

The most ambitious response to this body of work has come from a research consortium led by Dr Idris Okonkwo of the Australian Institute of Marine Science. Okonkwo's group has pioneered what it terms probiotic inoculation, in which heat-tolerant bacterial strains, isolated from corals that survived the 2016 and 2017 mass bleaching events, are introduced into laboratory-reared coral fragments before outplanting. In trials reported in 2024, inoculated fragments retained roughly 40 per cent more living tissue than control fragments during a simulated heat event of 33 degrees Celsius, although the differential narrowed when the stress was prolonged beyond ten days. Okonkwo has described the results as encouraging but provisional, noting that field-scale efficacy under variable oceanographic conditions has yet to be conclusively demonstrated.

Not every researcher in the field reads the evidence in this way. Professor Henrik Vogel, an evolutionary ecologist at Stockholm University, has emerged as the most articulate sceptic. Vogel does not contest the empirical findings; rather, he questions the inferential leap from controlled aquarium experiments to reef-scale intervention. In a 2023 review, his group argued that microbial assemblages on reefs are subject to such intense ecological turnover that any introduced strain is likely to be displaced or diluted within weeks, regardless of its laboratory performance. Vogel further objects, on precautionary grounds, that releasing cultured bacterial communities into open marine ecosystems may have consequences for non-target organisms that current monitoring protocols are ill-equipped to detect. The contrast with Okonkwo's optimism is sharp, although both researchers stress that they are debating timelines and risk thresholds rather than the underlying biology.

The policy dimension of this dispute has become increasingly visible. National adaptation strategies, particularly in small island states, have historically allocated resources to passive measures such as fishing restrictions and watershed management. Microbial intervention, by contrast, requires laboratory infrastructure, sustained funding for outplanting campaigns and a regulatory framework for releasing engineered organisms. Dr Mereani Tuilagi, an environmental policy specialist at the University of the South Pacific, has observed that the financial calculus is not straightforward. Although per-hectare costs of inoculation are still high, she argues, they may compare favourably with the alternative of accepting near-total reef collapse, provided that the technique can be shown to function at scale. Tuilagi is careful to add that this conditional remains, for the moment, unverified.

A further complication arises from the question of who decides. Several Pacific governments have indicated that any microbial intervention within their territorial waters should be subject to indigenous consultation, on the grounds that reefs are not merely ecological assets but elements of customary law and cultural identity. International conservation bodies have generally endorsed this position, although implementation has been uneven. A 2024 review by the International Union for Conservation of Nature noted that fewer than a third of pilot inoculation programmes had documented prior consent procedures that met the organisation's stated criteria. The report stopped short of recommending a moratorium, but it called for substantially enhanced governance before any expansion to commercial scale.

These disagreements feed into a broader argument about what climate adaptation should aim to preserve. Some researchers, including Okonkwo, treat the goal as the maintenance of functional reef ecosystems, even if their species composition shifts considerably from a historical baseline. Others, Vogel among them, argue that interventions designed to keep particular reef structures alive under conditions that exceed their evolutionary tolerances risk becoming open-ended commitments with no defensible exit point. The two positions, though framed in scientific language, reflect different judgements about acceptable transformation, and the empirical evidence on its own appears unable to adjudicate between them.

On the evidence available, the steadiest stance is one that refuses both technological optimism and reflexive alarm. The microbial turn has yielded genuine insights into how corals tolerate thermal stress, and there is a reasonable case for continued laboratory and small-scale field research. At the same time, the leap to widespread inoculation rests on inferences that, on Vogel's reading, have not yet been adequately tested at reef scale. The more pertinent question, on this writer’s account, is not whether microbial intervention works in principle but whether the governance architecture surrounding it can mature at the pace the underlying biology now seems to demand. Should that architecture fail to keep pace, the most promising techniques may either be deployed prematurely or set aside altogether, and neither outcome is likely to serve the reefs whose preservation motivates the debate in the first place.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture continues our marine pollution series — turning from oil-spill hydrocarbons to the much smaller, much harder-to-trace contaminant class we collectively label microplastics. [pause:5s] The conceptual platform I'll lean on is from the work of Professor Idris Onwuka — that's O-N-W-U-K-A, no hyphen, no diacritic. Onwuka's 2019 review redefined the field by collapsing earlier size-based taxonomies into what he calls "fragmentation cascade theory". [pause:3s] First, some historical orientation. The coastal sediment series I'll quote today was first sampled in 2009 — sorry, let me correct that, 2007; the descriptive synthesis was published in 2009 but the cores themselves were extracted in 2007. So whenever I reference the baseline sediment year, please record 2007. [pause:3s] Right. A brief tense-orientation. Onwuka's framework USED TO be tested by gravimetric mass alone — quite crude — NOW the field deploys infrared spectroscopy combined with pyrolysis mass-spec, and from 2028 a North-Atlantic consortium WILL be rolling out autonomous in-situ sampling drones. So past, present, future. For today's session I'm focusing on the CURRENT analytical regime — that is, the spectroscopy-plus-pyrolysis pairing. Moving to terminology. The contaminant class Onwuka foregrounds — particles below five millimetres in maximum dimension generated by environmental shedding rather than industrial design — is termed "secondary microplastic". Now, you'll meet related labels in the older literature: fragmentation debris, weathered residue, breakdown fines. All gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with Onwuka's term. The currently accepted scholarly term is secondary microplastic — s-e-c-o-n-d-a-r-y microplastic. So when the older corpus uses fragmentation debris or breakdown fines, that's a related but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to flag is what oceanographers call the "vertical partitioning gradient". When ecotoxicologists describe how microplastic concentrations distribute through the water column, they sketch a graded gradient running from surface buoyant films through neutrally-buoyant midwater suspensions to settled benthic deposits. So, you know, you'll find polyethylene flakes drifting on the slick at the air-water interface — that's the buoyant film. Or polystyrene beads that have absorbed enough biofilm to hang at thirty metres — that's neutrally-buoyant suspension. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical label. The umbrella term is the vertical partitioning gradient. [pause:3s] Now, the sediment-core data — and please pay close attention here, because the quantifiers cluster densely. Of the four hundred and sixty cores we processed across six estuaries last winter, MOST contained measurable secondary microplastic — roughly eighty-two per cent. Only a few — about six per cent — were beneath our detection threshold, and some — twelve per cent — showed ambiguous or contaminated readings we excluded. So contamination dominates numerically, but the clean-core tail, though small, is methodologically significant. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to introduce is "biofilm conditioning". This refers to the temporal process by which marine bacteria colonise a microplastic surface, altering its buoyancy and toxicity profile within days to weeks. At the Halifax estuary station, our team documented sixty-eight discrete conditioning trajectories across one quarterly sampling window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that larger plastic items pose proportionally greater ecological risk is, frankly, not supported. Most of the toxicity assays in our dataset did NOT show the predicted monotonic rise in tissue uptake as particle size increased. Quite the opposite — many showed a downward curve, with peak uptake clustering at the one-to-fifty-micrometre fraction. So the older "bigger-is-worse" hypothesis, which predicts linear risk scaling, is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to something I touched on earlier — the methodological tense-orientation point I opened with. That CURRENT spectroscopy-plus-pyrolysis state is what we're, sorta, gonna scrutinise in this afternoon's lab. I want you to focus on the pyrolysis fragment-identification protocols specifically, not the drone-sampling futures or the legacy gravimetric instruments. [pause:3s] To summarise: microplastic pollution operates as a fragmentation cascade, not a single source; the technical term for environmentally-shed particles below five millimetres is secondary microplastic; contamination dominates estuarine sediments at roughly eighty-two per cent; and the bigger-is-worse hypothesis is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine remediation pathways. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The line graph illustrates per-capita carbon dioxide emissions, in tonnes per person, in the United States, Germany, China and India over a fifty-year period from 1970 to 2020.

Overall, the two developed economies followed a clearly downward trajectory, whereas the two Asian economies moved in the opposite direction, with China rising most steeply of all. Despite this convergence, a substantial gap between the highest and lowest emitters persisted throughout the period.

In 1970, the United States led at 21.0 tonnes per head, with Germany some distance behind at 13.5. Both figures then fell steadily, reaching 14.2 and 7.7 tonnes respectively by 2020. China, by contrast, surged from a negligible 0.9 tonnes to roughly 7.4, climbing sharply after 2000 and almost matching Germany's 7.7 by the end of the period.

India rose far more modestly, edging up from just 0.4 to 1.9 tonnes across the five decades and remaining the lowest emitter by a wide margin. As a result, while the Western nations and China converged near 7 to 14 tonnes by 2020, India stayed firmly at the foot of the graph throughout.
The line graph charts per-capita carbon dioxide emissions, measured in tonnes per person, across the United States, Germany, China and India between 1970 and 2020.

Overall, the trajectories of the developed and developing economies diverged sharply: the Western nations registered a sustained decline, whereas the two Asian economies climbed, China's ascent being by far the most pronounced. Even so, a considerable disparity between the heaviest and lightest emitters endured across the half-century.

The American figure, the highest at the outset, eased from 21.0 tonnes per head in 1970 to 14.2 by 2020, while Germany's contracted more smoothly, from 13.5 to 7.7. China's experience inverted this pattern entirely: emissions rocketed from a negligible 0.9 tonnes to some 7.4, the curve climbing steeply after 2000 and converging upon Germany's 7.7 by the close of the period without quite overtaking it.

India, meanwhile, advanced only marginally, inching from 0.4 to a mere 1.9 tonnes and thereby anchoring the foot of the graph throughout. What emerges, then, is a striking realignment: the once-vast gulf between the West and China had all but closed by 2020, even as India's per-capita output remained an order of magnitude smaller.

There is widespread agreement that continuing to breach planetary boundaries will eventually prove far costlier than investing in prevention today.

Ordinary citizens can still do their bit by moderating consumption, even though systemic change ultimately rests with policymakers and industry.

blocks.text: While critics dismiss household recycling as a drop in the ocean, such habits can gradually shift social norms and build public appetite for bolder policy.
Although strict emissions targets are often praised, developing nations understandably decry them as a form of green protectionism that stalls their industrialisation.
It could be argued that a rapid phase-out of fossil fuels is reckless, yet the cost of inaction on wildfires and crop failure may ultimately prove far greater.
Some contend that renewable energy remains too intermittent to replace fossil fuels entirely, though storage technology is advancing quickly enough to narrow this gap.
As decarbonisation gains momentum, industries slow to adapt are likely to come under growing scrutiny from investors and regulators alike.
Advances in battery storage may soon make renewable power reliable enough to dominate national grids currently propped up by fossil fuels.
Consumers are expected to demand ever more transparency about a company's carbon footprint, rewarding brands that credibly commit to sustainable practices.
Should current emission trajectories persist, breaching further planetary boundaries could become the norm rather than the exception within a few decades.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas earlier generations treated arable land as an inexhaustible resource, today's policymakers must confront its finite and increasingly fragile nature.
Compared with the gradual environmental damage of the past, anthropogenic climate change today is unfolding at an unprecedented and accelerating pace.
Unlike the piecemeal environmental regulations of previous decades, current proposals for decarbonisation demand coordinated, economy-wide transformation.
Developed economies that industrialised on cheap fossil fuels are in a markedly different position from developing nations now urged to prioritise sustainable growth from the outset.
A case study of a mining region forced to confront mass unemployment illustrates the real human cost behind an abrupt fossil-fuel phase-out.
Longitudinal data tracking the plummeting cost of solar power can be cited to show that the economic case for delaying mitigation is weakening.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The accelerating climate crisis has provoked a polarised debate between those who demand decisive intervention without delay and those who caution that the economic price may be ruinous. While both positions carry weight, I am inclined to side with the camp pushing for rapid action.

Advocates of swift mitigation point to a mounting scientific consensus that the planet is approaching several tipping points. The IPCC has repeatedly warned that crossing the 1.5C threshold could trigger irreversible feedback loops, such as the collapse of ice sheets and the dieback of the Amazon. It is the catastrophic, non-linear nature of these risks that makes incrementalism so dangerous; once thresholds are breached, no amount of capital can buy the climate back. Moreover, the cost of inaction, from wildfires to crop failures and climate-driven displacement, arguably dwarfs the cost of transition.

On the other hand, sceptics argue that an abrupt pivot away from fossil fuels could devastate economies that still rely heavily on coal, oil and gas. Coal-producing regions in Poland or India, for instance, may suffer mass unemployment if mines are shuttered overnight, and developing nations contend that strict targets impose a hypocritical brake on their industrialisation. From this angle, the transition can look less like a moral imperative than a luxury the poor cannot afford.

In my view, these concerns are valid, but they argue for a just transition rather than no transition at all. Subsidies for green jobs, carbon dividends and technology transfers can soften the blow for vulnerable workers while still pursuing aggressive decarbonisation. To conclude, although the economic burden of climate action is undeniable, the cost of complacency is likely to be far greater, and a thoughtfully designed pathway can reconcile both priorities.

The question of whether climate action ought to be pursued aggressively, or moderated in deference to economic feasibility, has become one of the defining policy disputes of our era. Although the trade-offs are real, the weight of evidence inclines me towards the view that immediate action is not merely preferable but unavoidable.

Proponents of urgent mitigation draw on a robust body of climatological evidence indicating that anthropogenic warming is accelerating non-linearly. Should current emission trajectories persist, the cascading failure of permafrost, monsoonal systems and coral reefs could become unmanageable within decades. Particularly compelling is the asymmetry of risk: the upside of overreacting is a cleaner, more resilient economy, whereas the downside of underreacting may be civilisational. Furthermore, the plummeting cost of solar photovoltaics, down over seventy per cent in a decade, has rendered the economic case for delay markedly weaker.

Detractors, however, raise legitimate concerns about distributive justice. A precipitate phase-out of hydrocarbons would dislocate fossil-fuel-dependent communities and inflate energy bills for households already squeezed by inflation. Developing economies, in particular, contend that decarbonisation mandates issued by historically high-emitting nations amount to a form of green protectionism, since the very wealth now used to lecture them was accumulated through unrestrained industrial pollution. Not until these equity dimensions are seriously addressed will any global compact prove durable.

In my considered view, however, the dichotomy is largely false. What is required is not delay but a calibrated transition: front-loading investment in clean infrastructure, recycling carbon-pricing revenue into worker retraining, and shielding low-income households through targeted rebates. Such a framework converts climate policy from a zero-sum sacrifice into a long-run productivity dividend, since the industries that pioneer decarbonisation today are likely to dominate the markets of tomorrow. To conclude, although the economic friction of decarbonisation is non-trivial, the geophysical clock is unforgiving, and a well-engineered transition, rather than wholesale delay, offers the only credible path to reconciling planetary boundaries with prosperity.

blocks.text: TOPIC 08 - ENVIRONMENT: Describe an environmental change you'd like to see in your community
A. SENTENCE UPGRADE LADDER (Band 6 -> 7 -> 8)
Sentence 1
Band 6: A lot of people in my area throw rubbish into the river, and it makes the water very dirty.
Band 7: A considerable number of residents in my neighbourhood routinely dump household waste into the local river, which has severely polluted the water.

Band 8: What I find most distressing is the entrenched practice, prevalent among riverside residents, of indiscriminately discharging household refuse into the waterway - a behaviour that has rendered the river ecologically compromised and visibly contaminated.
Sentence 2
Band 6: I want the government to plant more trees in the city because the air is bad.
Band 7: I would like the local authorities to launch a large-scale tree-planting initiative, as the city's air quality has deteriorated significantly.

Band 8: Were the municipal authorities to spearhead an ambitious urban afforestation programme, the persistent anthropogenic air pollution choking our city centre could, in all likelihood, be substantially mitigated within a decade.
Sentence 3
Band 6: People should use less plastic so the environment is better.
Band 7: Residents ought to cut down on single-use plastics to alleviate the strain on the environment.

Band 8: It is the systemic reduction of single-use plastics - rather than tokenistic recycling campaigns - that holds genuine promise for reversing the proliferation of non-biodegradable waste in our community.
Sentence 4
Band 6: Climate change is a big problem and we need to do something.
Band 7: Climate change poses an unprecedented threat, and decisive action is urgently required at every level of society.
Band 8: Climate change, now widely acknowledged as the defining existential challenge of our epoch, demands a coordinated, multi-tiered response that transcends mere lip service from policymakers.
Sentence 5
Band 6: If we don't act now, the future will be very bad.
Band 7: Unless we take immediate action, future generations will inherit a severely degraded planet.
Band 8: Failing decisive intervention in the coming decade, we risk bequeathing to posterity a planet whose ecological damage may well prove irreversible.
B. CUE CARD + MODEL ANSWER
Cue Card:
Describe an environmental change you would like to see in your community.
You should say:
what the change is
why this change is needed
who would benefit from it
and explain how this change could be implemented.
Model Answer (260 words):

The environmental change I'd most like to witness in my community is the comprehensive transformation of our urban canal system - currently a notorious dumping ground - into a series of revitalised green corridors lined with native vegetation and accessible pedestrian walkways.

What prompts me to raise this issue is the sheer scale of degradation that has unfolded over the past two decades. Hanoi's To Lich River, which once meandered picturesquely through the old quarters, has been reduced to little more than an open sewer, exuding a stench that locals have grudgingly normalised. Not only does this constitute a glaring eyesore, but it also poses tangible public health risks, particularly for children and the elderly residing nearby.

Were such a regeneration project to be undertaken, the beneficiaries would be manifold. Local residents would reclaim a vital recreational space; small businesses fronting the canal could thrive on increased foot traffic; and, crucially, the urban heat island effect - exacerbated by rampant concretisation - would be substantially tempered through evapotranspiration from restored greenery.

Implementing such an ambitious overhaul would, admittedly, demand sustained political will and considerable capital. What I'd advocate is a phased, public-private partnership model, drawing inspiration from Seoul's Cheonggyecheon restoration, whereby a derelict elevated highway was dismantled to expose a once-buried stream. Funding could be sourced through green bonds, while community stewardship schemes would foster long-term ownership.

Ultimately, this isn't merely about aesthetics; it's about reasserting the principle that liveable cities and ecological integrity needn't be mutually exclusive - a principle our community urgently needs to embrace.

1. Governments are trying to find new ways to MITIGATE the harmful effects of rising sea levels on coastal communities. --- MITIGATE (động từ) = giảm thiểu, làm dịu bớt mức độ nghiêm trọng của một tác động tiêu cực; collocation phổ biến: "mitigate the effects of", "mitigate a risk"; đừng nhầm với "militate against" (cản trở).

2. The clearing of large areas of tropical forest is reducing the BIODIVERSITY found there. --- BIODIVERSITY (danh từ không đếm được) = đa dạng sinh học; collocation: "a loss of biodiversity", "biodiversity conservation"; không có dạng số nhiều.

3. Scientists warn that once certain ecosystems collapse, the damage will become completely IRREVERSIBLE. --- IRREVERSIBLE (tính từ) = không thể đảo ngược, không thể khắc phục; tiền tố phủ định là "ir-" (không phải "un-reversible"); collocation: "irreversible damage/consequences".

4. DEFORESTATION in the Amazon is one of the main drivers of global carbon emissions. --- DEFORESTATION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự phá rừng trên diện rộng; collocation: "massive/rampant deforestation", "curb deforestation"; phân biệt với "afforestation" (trồng rừng mới) và "reforestation" (trồng lại rừng).

5. URBAN SPRAWL is destroying natural habitats and farmland around the city. --- URBAN SPRAWL (danh từ không đếm được) = sự đô thị hoá tràn lan, thiếu kiểm soát; collocation: "unchecked urban sprawl", "urban sprawl encroaches on"; đối lập với "urban planning".

6. Flying less and eating locally produced food are two simple ways to reduce your CARBON FOOTPRINT. --- CARBON FOOTPRINT (danh từ ghép, đếm được) = tổng lượng khí thải nhà kính do một cá nhân/tổ chức gây ra; collocation: "reduce/calculate one's carbon footprint"; không viết tách "carbon-footprint" khi làm danh từ.

7. The steady DEPLETION of the region's groundwater supplies is threatening the long-term water security of local farmers. --- DEPLETION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự cạn kiệt dần một nguồn tài nguyên; luôn cần giới từ "of" khi nêu tài nguyên cụ thể ("the depletion of resources"); collocation: "resource depletion", "ozone depletion".

8. Decades of unchecked industrial pollution have caused severe DEGRADATION of the local wetland. --- DEGRADATION (danh từ không đếm được) = sự suy thoái, quá trình môi trường xuống cấp; collocation: "environmental/land degradation"; phân biệt với "biodegradable" (dễ phân huỷ sinh học, mang nghĩa tích cực).

9. Most climate scientists agree that the recent rise in global temperatures is largely ANTHROPOGENIC rather than the result of natural cycles. --- ANTHROPOGENIC (tính từ) = do con người gây ra; thuật ngữ học thuật trang trọng, có thể thay bằng "man-made"/"human-induced" trong văn nói; collocation: "anthropogenic warming/emissions".

10. The oil company's environmental record has recently COME UNDER SCRUTINY after the spill was made public. --- COME UNDER SCRUTINY (cụm động từ) = bị soi xét, giám sát chặt chẽ; collocation: "come under intense/public scrutiny"; "scrutiny" là danh từ không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều.

11. Researchers warn that the Arctic could soon reach a critical TIPPING POINT beyond which the ice loss becomes self-perpetuating and impossible to reverse. --- TIPPING POINT (danh từ ghép, đếm được) = điểm tới hạn gây ra thay đổi lớn, khó đảo ngược; luôn viết hai từ tách rời; collocation: "reach/cross a tipping point".

12. Several major economies have announced plans to PHASE OUT coal-fired power stations within the next two decades. --- PHASE OUT (cụm động từ) = loại bỏ dần theo lộ trình, không đột ngột; khi làm danh từ viết có gạch nối "a phase-out"; collocation: "phase out fossil fuels".
Phần B

1. Band 6: Factories put a lot of bad gases into the air and this makes global warming worse. - Band 7: Factories release substantial greenhouse gas emissions, which exacerbate global warming. - Band 8: It is the unchecked anthropogenic emissions pouring from industrial facilities that continue to drive global warming to increasingly alarming levels.

2. Band 6: If people keep cutting down trees, many animals will lose their homes. - Band 7: If deforestation continues at its current rate, countless species will lose their natural habitats. - Band 8: Were deforestation to persist unabated, the resulting loss of biodiversity would leave countless species with nowhere left to call home.

3. Band 6: The government should use more solar and wind power instead of coal. - Band 7: The government should invest more heavily in renewable energy sources such as solar and wind, rather than relying on coal. - Band 8: Not until the government commits to phasing out coal in favour of renewable energy will the country make any meaningful progress towards decarbonisation.

4. Band 6: Rich countries caused most of the pollution in the past, so they should help poorer countries now. - Band 7: Since developed nations are historically responsible for the majority of emissions, they ought to support developing countries in tackling climate change. - Band 8: Given that developed economies bear disproportionate historical responsibility for cumulative emissions, it is only equitable that they should shoulder the greater share of the burden in assisting developing nations to mitigate climate change.

5. Band 6: Plastic waste in the ocean is a very big problem and it is getting worse every year. - Band 7: Marine plastic pollution is a serious and worsening problem, with the scale of the crisis increasing year on year. - Band 8: What is most alarming is not merely the scale of marine plastic pollution but the rate at which it continues to escalate, with each passing year bringing the world closer to an ecological tipping point.

6. Band 6: One person recycling more will not really change the whole climate problem. - Band 7: An individual recycling more is, admittedly, just a drop in the ocean compared to the scale of the climate crisis. - Band 8: While one individual's efforts to recycle amount to little more than a drop in the ocean, it is only when such actions are replicated on a mass scale that they can meaningfully mitigate the climate crisis.

7. Band 6: Cities are growing too fast and this is destroying the countryside around them. - Band 7: Cities are expanding at an unsustainable rate, and this unchecked urban sprawl is encroaching on the surrounding countryside. - Band 8: So rapid has urban sprawl become that once-fertile arable land on the city's fringes is being irreversibly swallowed up by concrete and asphalt.

8. Band 6: If nothing changes soon, some of the damage to nature will never be fixed. - Band 7: Unless urgent action is taken, some of the damage inflicted on the natural environment will become irreversible. - Band 8: Failing swift and decisive intervention, we risk crossing tipping points beyond which the degradation of our ecosystems can never be undone.

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)
The Sixth Mass Extinction: Scientists warn that human activity has triggered a mass extinction event, with species dying out at 100 to 1,000 times the natural background rate.
The Plastic Epidemic: It is estimated that by 2050, there will be more plastic in the ocean than fish (by weight) due to the proliferation of single-use packaging.
Renewable Energy Surge: The cost of solar and wind power has plummeted by over 70% in the last decade, making renewable energy economically viable alternatives to fossil fuels.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: Who should solve environmental problems? (Governments vs. Individuals)

Government's Role: Only governments have the power to enact widespread legislation (e.g., banning disposable plastics, taxing carbon emissions); they can heavily subsidise renewable energy infrastructure on a national scale.

Individual's Role: Consumer demand drives corporate behaviour—if individuals boycott unethical companies and choose eco-friendly products, markets will shift; collective grassroots actions (recycling, reducing meat consumption) significantly lower the global carbon footprint.
Topic: Increasing the price of fuel (Should we heavily tax fossil fuels?)

Arguments FOR (Pros): It acts as a powerful financial deterrent, forcing people to use public transport or switch to electric vehicles; the tax revenue generated can be reinvested into green technologies and conservation projects.

Arguments AGAINST (Cons): It is a "regressive tax" that disproportionately harms low-income families who rely on cheap fuel for their daily commute; it drastically increases the cost of transporting basic goods, leading to nationwide inflation.
Topic: Economic Growth vs. Environmental Protection

Prioritising the Environment: A destroyed planet cannot support an economy; natural disasters caused by climate change already cost nations billions in damages; sustainable development creates new "green jobs."

Prioritising the Economy (Developing Nations' perspective): Developing countries need industrialisation to lift their citizens out of poverty; imposing strict environmental laws on them now is hypocritical, as wealthy nations already built their economies on fossil fuels.
(Câu điều kiện hỗn hợp - Cấu trúc siêu việt để diễn tả "Sự hối tiếc" về quá khứ dẫn đến hậu quả ở hiện tại, đặc biệt phù hợp cho chủ đề Môi trường)

B. CUE CARD + MODEL ANSWER
Cue Card:
Describe an environmental change you would like to see in your community.
You should say:
what the change is
why this change is needed
who would benefit from it
and explain how this change could be implemented.
Model Answer (260 words):

The environmental change I'd most like to witness in my community is the comprehensive transformation of our urban canal system - currently a notorious dumping ground - into a series of revitalised green corridors lined with native vegetation and accessible pedestrian walkways.

What prompts me to raise this issue is the sheer scale of degradation that has unfolded over the past two decades. Hanoi's To Lich River, which once meandered picturesquely through the old quarters, has been reduced to little more than an open sewer, exuding a stench that locals have grudgingly normalised. Not only does this constitute a glaring eyesore, but it also poses tangible public health risks, particularly for children and the elderly residing nearby.

Were such a regeneration project to be undertaken, the beneficiaries would be manifold. Local residents would reclaim a vital recreational space; small businesses fronting the canal could thrive on increased foot traffic; and, crucially, the urban heat island effect - exacerbated by rampant concretisation - would be substantially tempered through evapotranspiration from restored greenery.

Implementing such an ambitious overhaul would, admittedly, demand sustained political will and considerable capital. What I'd advocate is a phased, public-private partnership model, drawing inspiration from Seoul's Cheonggyecheon restoration, whereby a derelict elevated highway was dismantled to expose a once-buried stream. Funding could be sourced through green bonds, while community stewardship schemes would foster long-term ownership.

Ultimately, this isn't merely about aesthetics; it's about reasserting the principle that liveable cities and ecological integrity needn't be mutually exclusive - a principle our community urgently needs to embrace.
Q1: Should developing countries be required to reduce their emissions to the same extent as developed nations?

P (Point): I'd argue that holding developing countries to identical emission-reduction targets is fundamentally inequitable, although their long-term participation in decarbonisation is undeniably essential.

E (Explain): The principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities," enshrined in the UNFCCC framework, recognises that wealthy nations bear historical accountability for the cumulative carbon load currently warming the planet. Imposing uniform mandates effectively penalises poorer countries for industrialising belatedly.

E (Evidence): According to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (2023), the Global North - representing roughly 16% of the world's population - is responsible for approximately 79% of cumulative CO2 emissions since 1850. Furthermore, a peer-reviewed study published in Nature Sustainability Research on historical emissions responsibility suggests that high-income nations account for the majority of excess emissions beyond fair shares since 1960.

L (Link): Consequently, what's needed isn't uniformity but a calibrated approach - one where developed economies front the costs of green technology transfer, enabling developing nations to leapfrog the dirty-industrialisation phase entirely.
Q2: Can technology alone solve the climate crisis?

P (Point): While technological innovation is indispensable, the notion that technology alone can resolve climate change strikes me as dangerously naive - a form of techno-optimism that risks postponing the systemic behavioural changes we urgently need.

E (Explain): Solutions like carbon capture, direct air capture, and geoengineering, however promising, remain unproven at the scale required, and over-reliance on them creates moral hazard: people defer lifestyle changes, believing a technological saviour is imminent.

E (Evidence): A 2022 analysis in Nature Climate Change (Grant et al.) found that even the most optimistic deployment scenarios for direct air capture would offset less than 5% of current annual emissions by 2050. Conversely, the International Energy Agency's Net Zero by 2050 report (IEA, 2021) explicitly states that behavioural and demand-side changes must contribute around 8% of cumulative emission reductions - non-negotiably.
L (Link): What this suggests is that technology functions best as one pillar in a tripartite strategy alongside policy reform and behavioural transformation, rather than as a silver bullet.
Q3: How effectively can individuals make a difference to environmental problems?
P (Point): Individual actions, while frequently dismissed as inconsequential, do carry meaningful weight - particularly when aggregated and channelled through collective civic engagement.

E (Explain): The cynical refrain that "personal choices don't matter against corporate polluters" overlooks the fact that consumer demand, voting behaviour, and grassroots activism collectively shape the regulatory environment in which corporations operate.

E (Evidence): Research published in Environmental Research Letters (Ivanova et al., 2020) identified that household consumption accounts for approximately 72% of global greenhouse gas emissions, suggesting individual choices have substantial leverage. Moreover, a 2021 study in One Earth Research on individual climate action suggests that adopting high-impact behaviours - going car-free, eating plant-based, avoiding long-haul flights - can meaningfully reduce a person's annual carbon footprint.

L (Link): That said, individual action achieves transformative scale only when it galvanises political pressure - which is why I'd argue informed citizenship, rather than mere consumer virtue, is the genuine lever for change.

1. Section Type

blocks.text: 3. Predict 3 Ideas (before listening)
The lecturer will probably argue that gradualist models of climate change underestimate non-linear risk.
She may link planetary boundaries to a finite "safe operating space" for humanity.
She will likely contrast mitigation with adaptation, treating both as indispensable.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

> Good morning. Today I want to dismantle a quietly dangerous assumption that pervades policy discourse: that the climate will degrade in a linear, predictable fashion, giving us decades of polite warning. The Earth system, frankly, doesn't oblige.

> Let me anchor this in the planetary boundaries framework developed by Rockström and colleagues at the Stockholm Resilience Centre. Of nine biogeochemical thresholds — climate, biosphere integrity, freshwater, biogeochemical flows, and so on — six have already been transgressed. We are, in plain language, operating outside the safe corridor that permitted Holocene civilisation.

> Here's the uncomfortable subtlety. These boundaries are not slopes; they are cliffs. Crossing them activates so-called tipping points — self-reinforcing feedback loops that lock the planet into a new state. Consider the albedo flip: as Arctic sea ice retreats, darker ocean absorbs solar radiation that white ice would have reflected, amplifying warming further. Once enough ice is lost, the system cascades towards an ice-free summer regardless of subsequent emissions cuts. The lever, frankly, breaks in your hand.

> Which is why adaptation has moved from afterthought to architectural priority. Mitigation — cutting emissions — remains paramount, but emissions already in the atmosphere will warm the planet for centuries. Adaptation therefore means flood defences, drought-tolerant cultivars, managed retreat from indefensible coastlines, and what planners euphemistically call "climate-resilient infrastructure".

So, the adaptation finance gap. The UNEP Adaptation Gap Report puts developing-country needs at hundreds of billions of dollars annually this decade, against actual flows of roughly a tenth of that. But raw numbers, frankly, understate the cruelty of the distribution. Here is the moral fulcrum of the entire debate: the nations that have contributed least to cumulative emissions are, almost without exception, those facing the steepest physical exposure. The continent of Africa is responsible for under four per cent of historic carbon, yet bears a grossly disproportionate share of drought and crop failure. This is what ethicists mean by climate injustice — the decoupling of culpability from consequence. [pause]

What complicates this picture still further is a feedback loop the engineers don't model: the loss-and-damage threshold. Beyond a certain point, adaptation simply isn't possible. You cannot, um, build a sea wall tall enough for a nation like Tuvalu; you cannot irrigate a region whose aquifer has gone saline. At that frontier, adaptation quietly gives way to relocation, to the wrenching emergence of the climate refugee — a legal category, I'd note, that international law still scandalously refuses to recognise. [pause]

A further consideration, and it sharpens the albedo argument I raised earlier, is that tipping points are not independent. Cross one and you load the dice on the next — a destabilised Greenland ice sheet perturbs the Atlantic overturning circulation, which in turn shifts monsoon systems feeding a billion people. Lenton and colleagues call this a "tipping cascade", and it means our linear cost-benefit spreadsheets are, in a deep sense, mis-specified from the outset. [pause]

So when finance ministers haggle over a few billion in adaptation pledges, they are, whether they grasp it or not, pricing the habitability of entire territories. And that confrontation between accountancy and survival is exactly where I want to leave you — let me flag the key policy implication…

> One caveat, and it's a sharp one. Adaptation budgets globally are an order of magnitude below need, and maladaptation — interventions that worsen vulnerability — is rampant. Sea walls that displace flooding downstream are the classic case. Listen carefully now, because the next slide quantifies the adaptation finance gap rather brutally…

blocks.text: (e) Bài mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~182 từ)
The line graph illustrates per-capita carbon dioxide emissions, in tonnes per person, in the United States, Germany, China and India over a fifty-year period from 1970 to 2020.

Overall, the two developed economies followed a clearly downward trajectory, whereas the two Asian economies moved in the opposite direction, with China rising most steeply of all. Despite this convergence, a substantial gap between the highest and lowest emitters persisted throughout the period.

In 1970, the United States led at 21.0 tonnes per head, with Germany some distance behind at 13.5. Both figures then fell steadily, reaching 14.2 and 7.7 tonnes respectively by 2020. China, by contrast, surged from a negligible 0.9 tonnes to roughly 7.4, climbing sharply after 2000 and almost matching Germany's 7.7 by the end of the period.

India rose far more modestly, edging up from just 0.4 to 1.9 tonnes across the five decades and remaining the lowest emitter by a wide margin. As a result, while the Western nations and China converged near 7 to 14 tonnes by 2020, India stayed firmly at the foot of the graph throughout.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~192 từ)
The line graph charts per-capita carbon dioxide emissions, measured in tonnes per person, across the United States, Germany, China and India between 1970 and 2020.

Overall, the trajectories of the developed and developing economies diverged sharply: the Western nations registered a sustained decline, whereas the two Asian economies climbed, China's ascent being by far the most pronounced. Even so, a considerable disparity between the heaviest and lightest emitters endured across the half-century.

The American figure, the highest at the outset, eased from 21.0 tonnes per head in 1970 to 14.2 by 2020, while Germany's contracted more smoothly, from 13.5 to 7.7. China's experience inverted this pattern entirely: emissions rocketed from a negligible 0.9 tonnes to some 7.4, the curve climbing steeply after 2000 and converging upon Germany's 7.7 by the close of the period without quite overtaking it.

India, meanwhile, advanced only marginally, inching from 0.4 to a mere 1.9 tonnes and thereby anchoring the foot of the graph throughout. What emerges, then, is a striking realignment: the once-vast gulf between the West and China had all but closed by 2020, even as India's per-capita output remained an order of magnitude smaller.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng động từ phong phú hơn cho cùng dữ liệu ('eased', 'contracted', 'rocketed', 'inching', 'anchoring') và nominalisation ('China's ascent', 'a striking realignment'), nâng Lexical Resource.

•  Band 8 diễn đạt sự hội tụ tinh tế hơn ('the curve climbing steeply after 2000 and converging upon Germany's 7.7... without quite overtaking it') và kết bằng nhận định 'an order of magnitude smaller', thể hiện Grammatical Range cao hơn.

•  Đánh dấu điểm hội tụ (30s): Trung Quốc tăng dốc sau 2000 và gần bắt kịp Đức (7.4 vs 7.7) vào 2020 là chi tiết 'main feature' bắt buộc trích.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~284 words)

The accelerating climate crisis has provoked a polarised debate between those who demand decisive intervention without delay and those who caution that the economic price may be ruinous. While both positions carry weight, I am inclined to side with the camp pushing for rapid action.

Advocates of swift mitigation point to a mounting scientific consensus that the planet is approaching several tipping points. The IPCC has repeatedly warned that crossing the 1.5C threshold could trigger irreversible feedback loops, such as the collapse of ice sheets and the dieback of the Amazon. It is the catastrophic, non-linear nature of these risks that makes incrementalism so dangerous; once thresholds are breached, no amount of capital can buy the climate back. Moreover, the cost of inaction, from wildfires to crop failures and climate-driven displacement, arguably dwarfs the cost of transition.

On the other hand, sceptics argue that an abrupt pivot away from fossil fuels could devastate economies that still rely heavily on coal, oil and gas. Coal-producing regions in Poland or India, for instance, may suffer mass unemployment if mines are shuttered overnight, and developing nations contend that strict targets impose a hypocritical brake on their industrialisation. From this angle, the transition can look less like a moral imperative than a luxury the poor cannot afford.

In my view, these concerns are valid, but they argue for a just transition rather than no transition at all. Subsidies for green jobs, carbon dividends and technology transfers can soften the blow for vulnerable workers while still pursuing aggressive decarbonisation. To conclude, although the economic burden of climate action is undeniable, the cost of complacency is likely to be far greater, and a thoughtfully designed pathway can reconcile both priorities.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~318 words)

The question of whether climate action ought to be pursued aggressively, or moderated in deference to economic feasibility, has become one of the defining policy disputes of our era. Although the trade-offs are real, the weight of evidence inclines me towards the view that immediate action is not merely preferable but unavoidable.

Proponents of urgent mitigation draw on a robust body of climatological evidence indicating that anthropogenic warming is accelerating non-linearly. Should current emission trajectories persist, the cascading failure of permafrost, monsoonal systems and coral reefs could become unmanageable within decades. Particularly compelling is the asymmetry of risk: the upside of overreacting is a cleaner, more resilient economy, whereas the downside of underreacting may be civilisational. Furthermore, the plummeting cost of solar photovoltaics, down over seventy per cent in a decade, has rendered the economic case for delay markedly weaker.

Detractors, however, raise legitimate concerns about distributive justice. A precipitate phase-out of hydrocarbons would dislocate fossil-fuel-dependent communities and inflate energy bills for households already squeezed by inflation. Developing economies, in particular, contend that decarbonisation mandates issued by historically high-emitting nations amount to a form of green protectionism, since the very wealth now used to lecture them was accumulated through unrestrained industrial pollution. Not until these equity dimensions are seriously addressed will any global compact prove durable.

In my considered view, however, the dichotomy is largely false. What is required is not delay but a calibrated transition: front-loading investment in clean infrastructure, recycling carbon-pricing revenue into worker retraining, and shielding low-income households through targeted rebates. Such a framework converts climate policy from a zero-sum sacrifice into a long-run productivity dividend, since the industries that pioneer decarbonisation today are likely to dominate the markets of tomorrow. To conclude, although the economic friction of decarbonisation is non-trivial, the geophysical clock is unforgiving, and a well-engineered transition, rather than wholesale delay, offers the only credible path to reconciling planetary boundaries with prosperity.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8

•  Band 8 dùng cấu trúc cao cấp dày đặc (đảo ngữ 'Should current trajectories persist', 'Not until... will...', cleft ngầm 'What is required is...') trong khi Band 7 chỉ dùng một cleft 'It is the catastrophic... nature... that...'.

•  Band 8 nâng lexis lên bậc Band 8 ('anthropogenic warming', 'cascading failure', 'asymmetry of risk', 'precipitate phase-out', 'green protectionism', 'productivity dividend') và nominalisation dày, vượt hẳn cụm hơi đời thường 'price tag may be ruinous' của bản 7.

•  Band 8 phá thế lưỡng phân ('the dichotomy is largely false') thay vì chỉ chọn phe, và cohesion mượt hơn ('Furthermore', 'in particular', 'Such a framework'), nâng Task Response và Coherence lên một bậc.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
e- (ra ngoài) + mit (gửi, gốc Latin 'mittere') → emissions = những thứ được "gửi ra" khí quyển.
vocabulary.common_error: Thường dùng ở số nhiều 'emissions' khi nói về khí thải; dạng số ít 'emission' chỉ hành động phát ra một lần cụ thể.
vocabulary.definition_en: gases or other substances released into the atmosphere, typically produced by burning fuels
vocabulary.definition_vi: khí thải (thường do đốt nhiên liệu)
vocabulary.example: The amount of carbon emissions produced by factories is driving global warming.
vocabulary.memory_hook: e- (ra ngoài) + mit (gửi, gốc Latin 'mittere') → emissions = những thứ được 'gửi ra' khí quyển.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bền vững, có thể duy trì lâu dài mà không làm cạn kiệt tài nguyên thiên nhiên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Achieving environmental **sustainability** is a key goal for the next decade.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
sustain (duy trì) + -able (có thể) → có thể duy trì lâu dài mà không cạn kiệt.
vocabulary.common_error: Không dùng *sustainable* như từ khen chung; cần nêu rõ điều gì có thể duy trì lâu dài về môi trường, xã hội hoặc tài chính.
vocabulary.definition_en: capable of being maintained at a steady level without exhausting natural resources or causing damage
vocabulary.definition_vi: bền vững (không làm cạn kiệt tài nguyên)
vocabulary.example: Achieving environmental sustainability is a key goal for the next decade.
vocabulary.memory_hook: sustain (duy trì) + -able (có thể) → có thể duy trì lâu dài mà không cạn kiệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự phá rừng trên diện rộng, thường do hoạt động của con người gây ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Massive **deforestation** in the Amazon is severely affecting the world's oxygen supply.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (loại bỏ) + forest (rừng) + -ation → hành động loại bỏ rừng.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'deforestation' (phá rừng) với 'afforestation' (trồng rừng mới trên đất trống) hoặc 'reforestation' (trồng lại rừng đã mất).
vocabulary.definition_en: the clearing or removal of forests on a large scale, usually caused by human activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự phá rừng, nạn chặt phá rừng
vocabulary.example: Massive deforestation in the Amazon is severely affecting the world's oxygen supply.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (loại bỏ) + forest (rừng) + -ation → hành động loại bỏ rừng.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đất có thể trồng trọt, canh tác được (đất nông nghiệp).

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We are losing **arable** land as droughts deplete the soil that is good for growing crops.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
arable nghe gần 'arate' (Latin: cày) → đất có thể cày cấy, trồng trọt.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Arable' chỉ mô tả đất dùng để trồng trọt (cây lương thực), không dùng cho đất chăn thả gia súc (pasture/grazing land).
vocabulary.definition_en: (of land) suitable for or used for growing crops
vocabulary.definition_vi: (đất) có thể canh tác, trồng trọt được
vocabulary.example: We are losing arable land as droughts deplete the soil that is good for growing crops.
vocabulary.memory_hook: arable nghe gần 'arate' (Latin: cày) → đất có thể cày cấy, trồng trọt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự mở rộng thiếu kiểm soát của đô thị vào vùng nông thôn xung quanh, thường phá huỷ môi trường sống tự nhiên.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Cities are growing too fast, and unchecked **urban sprawl** is encroaching on the surrounding countryside.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
sprawl (nằm dài, lan ra) + urban (đô thị) → đô thị "lan" ra một cách thiếu kiểm soát.
vocabulary.common_error: *Urban sprawl* là danh từ không đếm được chỉ sự lan rộng thiếu kiểm soát; không dùng *an urban sprawl* trong nghĩa chung.
vocabulary.definition_en: the uncontrolled expansion of urban areas into the surrounding countryside, often destroying natural habitats
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự đô thị hoá tràn lan, lấn chiếm vùng nông thôn
vocabulary.example: Cities are growing too fast, and unchecked urban sprawl is encroaching on the surrounding countryside.
vocabulary.memory_hook: sprawl (nằm dài, lan ra) + urban (đô thị) → đô thị 'lan' ra một cách thiếu kiểm soát.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự giảm thiểu, hành động làm giảm mức độ nghiêm trọng của một tác động tiêu cực.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Climate-change **mitigation** requires coordinated policy action from every major economy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
mitigate (giảm nhẹ) + -ion → danh từ chỉ hành động/quá trình giảm nhẹ tác động.
vocabulary.common_error: Phân biệt 'mitigation' (hành động giảm nhẹ tác động, ví dụ giảm phát thải) với 'adaptation' (thích nghi với hậu quả đã xảy ra) — hai chiến lược khí hậu khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: action taken to reduce the severity, seriousness or harmful effects of something
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự giảm thiểu (tác động tiêu cực)
vocabulary.example: Climate-change mitigation requires coordinated policy action from every major economy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: mitigate (giảm nhẹ) + -ion → danh từ chỉ hành động/quá trình giảm nhẹ tác động.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tổng lượng khí thải nhà kính mà một cá nhân, tổ chức hay hoạt động gây ra.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Flying less and eating local produce are effective ways to reduce your **carbon footprint**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
footprint (dấu chân) + carbon → dấu vết khí thải các-bon mà mỗi hoạt động "để lại" trên hành tinh.
vocabulary.common_error: Dùng *reduce/cut one’s carbon footprint*; không nhầm với toàn bộ tác động môi trường và không nói *carbon footstep*.
vocabulary.definition_en: the total amount of greenhouse gases produced directly or indirectly by a person, organisation or activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: dấu chân các-bon (tổng lượng khí thải nhà kính do một cá nhân/tổ chức gây ra)
vocabulary.example: Flying less and eating local produce are effective ways to reduce your carbon footprint.
vocabulary.memory_hook: footprint (dấu chân) + carbon → dấu vết khí thải các-bon mà mỗi hoạt động 'để lại' trên hành tinh.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự cạn kiệt dần một nguồn tài nguyên cho đến khi gần như không còn lại gì.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> We must stop the rapid **depletion** of our natural resources before it's too late.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (bớt đi) + plete (gốc Latin 'plere' = đầy) → làm vơi dần cho đến khi cạn.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Depletion' là danh từ, cần giới từ 'of': 'the depletion of resources', không viết 'depletion resources'.
vocabulary.definition_en: the reduction in the amount of something, especially a natural resource, until little or none remains
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự cạn kiệt (tài nguyên thiên nhiên)
vocabulary.example: We must stop the rapid depletion of our natural resources before it's too late.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (bớt đi) + plete (gốc Latin 'plere' = đầy) → làm vơi dần cho đến khi cạn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Hệ sinh thái, cộng đồng sinh vật tương tác với môi trường vật lý xung quanh.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Policy must reconcile prosperity with protecting every fragile **ecosystem** we depend on.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
eco- (môi trường) + system (hệ thống) → hệ thống sinh vật và môi trường sống gắn kết với nhau.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Ecosystem' viết liền một từ trong tiếng Anh Anh chuẩn, không tách thành 'eco system' hay gạch nối 'eco-system'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a biological community of interacting organisms and their physical environment
vocabulary.definition_vi: hệ sinh thái
vocabulary.example: A supportive home can foster close bonds, just as a healthy ecosystem depends on the balance between every species within it.
vocabulary.memory_hook: eco- (môi trường) + system (hệ thống) → hệ thống sinh vật và môi trường sống gắn kết với nhau.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự suy thoái, quá trình môi trường bị xuống cấp về chất lượng.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Environmental **degradation** caused by decades of unchecked pollution has left the local river ecologically compromised.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (đi xuống) + grade (cấp độ) → chất lượng đi xuống từng bậc.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'degradation' (sự suy thoái) với 'biodegradable' (tự phân hủy) — 'degrade' trong ngữ cảnh môi trường ô nhiễm mang nghĩa tiêu cực, còn 'biodegradable' lại là tính chất tích cực (dễ phân hủy sinh học).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of something being made worse in quality or condition, especially damage to the natural environment
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự suy thoái (môi trường)
vocabulary.example: Environmental degradation caused by decades of unchecked pollution has left the local river ecologically compromised.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (đi xuống) + grade (cấp độ) → chất lượng đi xuống từng bậc.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Có thể tái tạo, không bị cạn kiệt khi sử dụng (như năng lượng mặt trời, gió).

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Solar power is a clean, **renewable** source of energy that we should invest in.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
re- (lại) + new (mới) → nguồn năng lượng có thể "làm mới" lại liên tục, không cạn.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi là tính từ cần danh từ theo sau (*renewable energy/resources*); danh từ số nhiều *renewables* chỉ các nguồn/năng lượng tái tạo trong ngữ cảnh chuyên môn.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of energy or resources) able to be replenished naturally and therefore not depleted when used
vocabulary.definition_vi: có thể tái tạo (năng lượng, tài nguyên)
vocabulary.example: Solar power is a clean, renewable source of energy that we should invest in.
vocabulary.memory_hook: re- (lại) + new (mới) → nguồn năng lượng có thể 'làm mới' lại liên tục, không cạn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Do con người gây ra, thường dùng để nói về ô nhiễm hoặc biến đổi khí hậu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> A robust body of climatological evidence indicates that **anthropogenic** warming is accelerating non-linearly.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
anthropo- (con người, như 'anthropology') + -genic (gây ra bởi) → do bàn tay con người tạo ra.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Anthropogenic' là thuật ngữ học thuật trang trọng; trong văn nói thông thường có thể thay bằng 'man-made' hoặc 'human-induced' để tránh nghe quá cứng nhắc.
vocabulary.definition_en: originating from human activity, especially referring to environmental pollution or change
vocabulary.definition_vi: do con người gây ra (thường nói về ô nhiễm, biến đổi khí hậu)
vocabulary.example: A robust body of climatological evidence indicates that anthropogenic warming is accelerating non-linearly.
vocabulary.memory_hook: anthropo- (con người, như 'anthropology') + -genic (gây ra bởi) → do bàn tay con người tạo ra.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Bị soi xét, chỉ trích hoặc giám sát chặt chẽ.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The issue of fossil-fuel subsidies has **come under** intense scrutiny, as experts grapple with how to phase them out fairly.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'scrutiny' gần 'scrutinise' (soi xét kỹ) → come under scrutiny = bị đưa ra "soi" dưới kính hiển vi dư luận.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Scrutiny' là danh từ không đếm được, không có dạng số nhiều 'scrutinies' trong nghĩa thông thường này.
vocabulary.definition_en: to start being examined or investigated very closely and critically
vocabulary.definition_vi: bị soi xét, bị giám sát chặt chẽ
vocabulary.example: The issue of fossil-fuel subsidies has come under intense scrutiny, as experts grapple with how to phase them out fairly.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'scrutiny' gần 'scrutinise' (soi xét kỹ) → come under scrutiny = bị đưa ra 'soi' dưới kính hiển vi dư luận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Một hành động hay đóng góp quá nhỏ so với quy mô của vấn đề lớn — như muối bỏ bể.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Banning plastic straws is just **a drop in the ocean** compared to the massive scale of industrial waste.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Một giọt nước (a drop) rơi vào cả đại dương (the ocean) → quá nhỏ để tạo ra khác biệt.
collocations: just a drop in the ocean
a drop in the ocean compared to
vocabulary.common_error: Idiom này luôn có mạo từ 'a' và giới từ 'in': 'a drop in the ocean', không nói 'a drop of the ocean'.
vocabulary.definition_en: an amount that is so small or insignificant that it makes almost no difference to a much larger problem
vocabulary.definition_vi: như muối bỏ bể, chỉ là một phần rất nhỏ không đáng kể
vocabulary.example: Banning plastic straws is just a drop in the ocean compared to the massive scale of industrial waste.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Một giọt nước (a drop) rơi vào cả đại dương (the ocean) → quá nhỏ để tạo ra khác biệt.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Phần nhỏ, dễ thấy của một vấn đề lớn hơn nhiều vẫn đang ẩn giấu bên dưới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The recent devastating floods are just **the tip of the iceberg** of climate change impacts.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Tảng băng trôi (iceberg) chỉ lộ phần đỉnh (tip) trên mặt nước, phần lớn chìm dưới biển → vấn đề thật lớn hơn nhiều so với những gì thấy được.
collocations: just the tip of the iceberg
the tip of the iceberg of a problem
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn có mạo từ xác định kép: 'the tip of the iceberg', không bỏ 'the' ở đâu cả.
vocabulary.definition_en: a small, visible part of a much larger problem that remains mostly hidden
vocabulary.definition_vi: phần nổi của tảng băng chìm, chỉ là dấu hiệu nhỏ của vấn đề lớn hơn nhiều
vocabulary.example: The recent devastating floods are just the tip of the iceberg of climate change impacts.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Tảng băng trôi (iceberg) chỉ lộ phần đỉnh (tip) trên mặt nước, phần lớn chìm dưới biển → vấn đề thật lớn hơn nhiều so với những gì thấy được.
synonyms: a small fraction of the problem

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Loại bỏ dần một thứ gì đó theo lộ trình, không dừng đột ngột.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Many developed countries plan to **phase out** petrol and diesel cars by 2030.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
phase (giai đoạn) + out (ra ngoài) → loại bỏ dần qua từng giai đoạn, không đột ngột.
vocabulary.common_error: Khi dùng làm danh từ phải viết có gạch nối 'phase-out' ('a gradual phase-out'); khi là động từ thì tách rời 'phase out'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to gradually stop using, producing or providing something over a period of time
vocabulary.definition_vi: loại bỏ dần, ngừng sử dụng theo lộ trình
vocabulary.example: Many developed countries plan to phase out petrol and diesel cars by 2030.
vocabulary.memory_hook: phase (giai đoạn) + out (ra ngoài) → loại bỏ dần qua từng giai đoạn, không đột ngột.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Góp một phần nhỏ công sức của bản thân vào một nỗ lực chung.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Everyone should **do their bit** for the environment by recycling and using public transport.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'bit' (một mẩu nhỏ) → mỗi người làm "một mẩu" phần việc của mình để góp thành nỗ lực chung.
collocations: do your bit for the environment
vocabulary.common_error: Sở hữu cách phải khớp với chủ ngữ: 'I do my bit', 'they do their bit' — không dùng cố định 'do one's bit' trong câu thực tế.
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a reasonable individual contribution to a shared or collective effort
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm phần việc nhỏ của mình, góp một phần công sức
vocabulary.example: Everyone should do their bit for the environment by recycling and using public transport.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'bit' (một mẩu nhỏ) → mỗi người làm 'một mẩu' phần việc của mình để góp thành nỗ lực chung.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Ngưỡng tới hạn mà chỉ cần một thay đổi nhỏ cũng có thể gây ra biến đổi lớn, khó đảo ngược.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Scientists warn that crossing certain **tipping points** could trigger irreversible feedback loops.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'tip' (làm nghiêng, đổ) → điểm mà chỉ cần đẩy nhẹ là cả hệ thống "đổ" sang trạng thái mới.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Tipping point' luôn viết hai từ tách rời, không viết liền 'tippingpoint'; số nhiều là 'tipping points'.
vocabulary.definition_en: a critical threshold beyond which a small change triggers a large, often irreversible, self-perpetuating shift
vocabulary.definition_vi: điểm tới hạn, ngưỡng gây ra thay đổi lớn không thể đảo ngược
vocabulary.example: Scientists warn that crossing certain tipping points could trigger irreversible feedback loops.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'tip' (làm nghiêng, đổ) → điểm mà chỉ cần đẩy nhẹ là cả hệ thống 'đổ' sang trạng thái mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Những ranh giới an toàn cho các hệ thống của Trái Đất, vượt qua sẽ gây rủi ro thay đổi lớn, khó đảo ngược.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Policy must reconcile prosperity with the **planetary boundaries** we cannot safely breach.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
planetary (thuộc hành tinh) + boundaries (ranh giới) → những ranh giới an toàn mà cả hành tinh không nên vượt qua.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn dùng số nhiều 'boundaries' vì khái niệm này bao gồm nhiều ranh giới khác nhau (khí hậu, đa dạng sinh học, nước ngọt...), không nói 'a planetary boundary' khi ám chỉ cả khung lý thuyết.
vocabulary.definition_en: the safe operating limits for key Earth-system processes, beyond which the risk of large-scale, irreversible environmental change increases sharply
vocabulary.definition_vi: ranh giới hành tinh (giới hạn an toàn cho các hệ thống Trái Đất)
vocabulary.example: Policy must reconcile prosperity with the planetary boundaries we cannot safely breach.
vocabulary.memory_hook: planetary (thuộc hành tinh) + boundaries (ranh giới) → những ranh giới an toàn mà cả hành tinh không nên vượt qua.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quá trình giảm hoặc loại bỏ phát thải các-bon khỏi nền kinh tế hay ngành công nghiệp.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Aggressive **decarbonisation** would dislocate communities still dependent on coal and oil.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
de- (loại bỏ) + carbon (các-bon) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình loại bỏ các-bon khỏi nền kinh tế.
vocabulary.common_error: Chú ý chính tả tiếng Anh Anh: 'decarbonisation' (-isation), không viết kiểu Mỹ 'decarbonization' (-ization).
vocabulary.definition_en: the process of reducing or eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from an economy, industry or activity
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự khử các-bon (loại bỏ phát thải các-bon khỏi nền kinh tế)
vocabulary.example: Aggressive decarbonisation would dislocate communities still dependent on coal and oil.
vocabulary.memory_hook: de- (loại bỏ) + carbon (các-bon) + -isation (quá trình) → quá trình loại bỏ các-bon khỏi nền kinh tế.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Chưa từng có tiền lệ, chưa từng xảy ra trước đây ở quy mô như vậy.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> These extreme weather changes are **unprecedented**, with events occurring on a scale never seen before.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
un- (không) + precedent (tiền lệ) + -ed → không có tiền lệ nào từng xảy ra trước đó.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'unprecedented' (chưa từng có tiền lệ) với 'unpredictable' (khó dự đoán) — hai từ có hình thức gần giống nhưng nghĩa khác nhau.
vocabulary.definition_en: never having happened, existed or been done before
vocabulary.definition_vi: chưa từng có tiền lệ, chưa từng xảy ra trước đây
vocabulary.example: These extreme weather changes are unprecedented, with events occurring on a scale never seen before.
vocabulary.memory_hook: un- (không) + precedent (tiền lệ) + -ed → không có tiền lệ nào từng xảy ra trước đó.
